b: That a smidge over one month of 2026 remains baffles me. It feels like just last Tuesday, the compelling on- and offstage drama in Mixed Feelings captured my attention in a bookstore aisle. I swear only a Sunday ago I, inspired by Instant Noodles and Beyond, collected ingredients to prepare “Ramyeon Egg” and “Shrimp Tom Yum Ramyeon.” And how has six months passed since my comfort watch To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before arrived in its gulpable graphic novel format? With that said, narrowing down this list proved challenging, especially after finishing five-star read after five-star read.

Before we leap into our bookish goals for 2027, let’s pause to appreciate some luminous stars in graphic novels, graphic nonfiction, and comics published over the year, including three selections from fellow Book Riot writers. Read on for a chuckle-out-loud university freshman story, romance, science fiction, and more.
2 of My Favorite Graphic Novels and Memoirs from 2026
Lindsey Cheng Dates a White Boy!!! by Asia Miller

At college during the 2010s, Lindsey Cheng carries an artsy tote and plays drums in an unnamed band with her besties, Mel and V. While her mother constantly requests her location and reminds her to study hard and limit socializing to the weekend, she begins dating Jason, a white indie rocker with a lot of opinions. Between toiling away in the library, roof-sitting during a party, and receiving pep talks from her friends, the lovable protagonist learns that she, in fact, emanates coolness. Not her boyfriend. As soon as I opened this hilarious book, I kept it close in my tote to pore over while awaiting my latte and between errands.
Until We Meet Again by Lily Kim Qian

Exploring belonging, family, mental health, and stability, this debut graphic memoir follows Lily, whose parents divorce then share custody. When her mother vanishes, Lily and her father pack up for Vancouver. Almost as soon as Lily makes friends, her dad uproots them. Relocating becomes a “force of habit”: “I got used to the notion that nothing would stay long in my life.” At 10, Lily has moved four times to various Canadian cities, and they eventually leave for Shanghai after her mom keeps resurfacing. The stunning illustrations feature a mesmerizing color palette of yellow, coral, turquoise, purple, and blues, and so many images—the shed antler, the tide pools—float in my mind.
3 of Book Rioters’ Favorite Graphic Novels and Comics from 2026

2026 has been my year of being obsessed with Heartstopper, and as such, I read a lot of books this year that claimed to be for fans of the series. Encore! is one of the very few that lives up to the comparison. First of all, the art is gorgeous. The second-chance romance is also very sweet: Clay and Aron used to be best friends, until they had a falling out. When they are paired up in a theater class, old feelings come to the surface. This is definitely one for the queer theater kids, and I loved the supportive friend group that rounds out the cast. If you need a pick-me-up, add this YA graphic novel romance to your TBR. —Danika Ellis

Anyone who has talked to me for more than five minutes in 2026 knows I’ve been obsessed with Heartstopper this year. Starting as a webcomic in 2016, the series came to a close with a final volume and a movie adaptation that both came out in July. It’s hard to overstate how beloved this story is, so there was a lot of pressure, after 10 years, to bring it to a satisfactory close. Luckily, Volume 6 does just that. Alice Oseman’s illustrations are stunning, and the story explores both main characters’ mental health struggles as Nick prepares to leave for university. This series means so much to me, as I know it does for many queer fans. —Danika Ellis

Brooding Prince Orion has never felt like he fits in among the beautiful, joyous gods of New Genesis. Then he learns the horrifying truth: he is the son of Darkseid, cruel tyrant of the planet Apokolips, and evil runs in his veins. Jack Kirby left some big shoes to fill when he created his magnum opus in 1971, and just as she did with 2024’s Barda, Ngozi Ukazu steps into those shoes ably, bringing complexity and humor to Kirby’s blunt characterization (and adding multiple women to a largely male cast). This earnest, epic bildungsroman is a great jumping-on point for new readers and a note-perfect take on Orion for longtime New Gods fans. —Jessica Plummer

If you crave more of the best, seek out our Best of the Century (So Far) series—especially the Best Comics of the Century, the graphic novels Rioters adored at this year’s midpoint, and the entirety of the Best Books of 2026.
